text: to 32° to 34° has been recommended3-6 in unconscious adults whose initial rhythm was ventricular fibrillation. Specific guidelines for the different types of arrhythmia are as follows. Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachy- cardia are treated in the same way. The guidelines for adults emphasise that the first defibrillating shock must be given as quickly as possible, although a short period of CPR may be appropriate first if the arrest was not wit- nessed. In cases of witnessed cardiac arrest a precordial thump, which sometimes aborts the arrhythmia if given within 30 seconds of the loss of cardiac output, may be given before attaching the monitor/defibrillator, but the at- tachment of the defibrillator must not be delayed. Al- though a strategy of three initial shocks has been the stand- ard, it is now recommended that a single shock is given, since this appears to be as effective as three shocks while minimising the interruption to chest compressions. Monophasic or biphasic shocks may be given, depending on the equipment available. For monophasic devices, the recommended energy for all shocks is 360J. For biphasic devices the optimum energy varies; in the UK and Europe an initial shock of 150-200J is recommended, with subse- quent shocks of 150-360J, but in other countries devices using lower energies may be available. After the initial shock, CPR should be immediately re- sumed for 2 minutes before reassessing the rhythm; a fur- ther shock should then be given if indicated, followed by immediate resumption of CPR, and this cycle of assess- ment, shock, and CPR should be continued throughout re- suscitation. At the same time, drug therapy may be started. In the UK and Europe, adrenaline 1 mg intravenously is recommended before the third shock, repeated every 3 to 5 minutes (roughly every 2 cycles) while resuscitation continues; in the USA, adrenaline may be started before the second or third shock. If the intravenous route is not available, the same dose may be given by intraosseous in- jection. Endotracheal dosage is a further alternative; doses 2 to 3 times greater than those given intravenously are sug- gested, although studies investigating this route have had mixed results.10,11 A single dose of vasopressin (as ar- gipressin) 40 units intravenously may be given instead of the first or second dose of adrenaline,4 but this is not uni- versally recommended.5,6 Amiodarone may be given be- fore the fourth shock (before the third or fourth shock in the USA); lidocaine is an alternative if amiodarone is not available. Other drugs (such as those described above) may be used as appropriate. Cycles of CPR, shocks, and adrenaline should continue for as long as defibrillation is indicated.
